    Reproduction study · computational drug discovery

    NetPert: prioritising targets with network response functions

    Reimplementation and robustness analysis of PLOS Computational Biology (2024) · paper · official code

    Scope, stated plainly. The real databases NetPert uses (IID, TRRUST, MGI, UniProt, Drug Repurposing Hub) could not be downloaded in the sandbox. Everything below is therefore a simulated-network benchmark on simulated scale-free networks with known ground truth. It validates the algorithm and its robustness; it makes no biological or drug-target claims. The same code can be re-run on the real Twist1 network once the data is available.
    Key findings (simulated networks only).
    • My vectorised implementation matches the official netpert.py weight functions to about 1e−16 on 45 simulated networks, including directed ones.
    • Against a shortest-path ground truth (see the correction below), NetPert recovers planted mediators best on scale-free, random and small-world networks (AUROC 0.96–1.00) but is beaten by driver personalised PageRank on modular networks (0.77 vs 0.91).
    • It concentrates its score: the top 10 genes hold 67% of the total weight, against 47% for betweenness.
    • Its ranking is more fragile than the baselines under degree-preserving rewiring (ρ = 0.31 vs 0.69 for betweenness at 1.6 swaps per edge).
    • With an independent cascade-knockout ground truth and the paper's own comparators (section 20), NetPert still has the best AUROC on scale-free networks (0.90 vs 0.89 for out-degree and 0.82 for the paper's betweenness), but the margin is small. It trails the paper's betweenness on precision@20 (0.64 vs 0.76) and out-degree on rank correlation (0.47 vs 0.57).
    • When the observed network is degraded (section 21), NetPert's accuracy drops faster than out-degree's: its AUROC lead disappears by 20% of edges removed and reverses at 40% (0.77 vs 0.82).
    • Replicating the experiments with the independent truth (section 22): NetPert is best with short, clean response lists (AUROC 0.97 at 3 responses) but loses its lead once 25% of the responses are false (0.82 vs 0.89 for out-degree).
    • Real-data result now available: the Twist1 run completed — see section 0 above.
    Correction to sections 3–11 and the scorecard. Those benchmarks use a shortest-path ground truth. I later found that this truth is exactly the set of genes with a non-zero score under the paper’s own driver-to-response betweenness comparator, which therefore scores AUROC 1.000 against it by construction; it favours path-based methods in general. Section 20 repeats the benchmark with an independent ground truth (simulated cascade knockouts) and the paper’s own comparators run through the official code. There, NetPert’s advantage is much smaller and not uniform, so treat the margins in the earlier sections as optimistic.

    1. Methods

    1.1 Network and notation

    The vertex set contains the driver gene a, R response genes b and the intermediate genes, N vertices in total. Interactions are directed edges u → v. The adjacency matrix is stored as Avu = 1 when the edge u → v exists (destination first, as in getLaplacian), and the Laplacian is L = Dout − A, where Dout holds out-degrees. Every column of L sums to zero, so the dynamics below conserve total activity.

    1.2 Response dynamics

    The driver is given unit activity and activity spreads by linear diffusion, dx/dt = −L x, with solution x(t) = G(t) x(0) and Green's function G(t) = exp(−tL). The entry Gxa(t) is the activity at gene x at time t after perturbing a. Because G is a matrix exponential, G(T) = G(T−t) G(t) for any 0 ≤ t ≤ T.

    1.3 Time scale (relaxation parameter r)

    At short times the driver's activity decays at rate kout(a). The code picks the total time T = ntΔt so that, to leading order, driver activity falls by the fraction r: Δt = −ln(1−r) / (kout(a) · nt). The defaults are r = 0.5 and nt = 16.

    1.4 Gene weight

    For intermediate gene x, the unnormalised weight sums over responses the time integral of "activity reaches x from the driver at time t, then reaches the response in the remaining time":

    W(x) = Σb ∫0T Gbx(T−t) Gxa(t) dt,   w(x) = W(x) / Σy W(y).

    By the semigroup property, summing the integrand over all genes x gives Gba(T) at every t. So w(x) is the time-averaged share of driver-to-response influence that is routed through x. This is a mechanistic ranking: genes that sit on many short, well-connected routes between the driver and the responses score highly, whatever their global connectivity. As in the reference code, the driver and the response currently being scored are excluded from its own term, and weights are normalised to sum to 1.

    1.5 Numerics and complexity

    G(ti) for i = 0…16 is built from one matrix exponential exp(−Δt L) (scipy.linalg.expm) and repeated multiplication. The 17-point grid fits Romberg quadrature (scipy.integrate.romb), which needs 2k+1 samples. My implementation contracts all responses and genes in one tensor operation. Cost is O(nt N3) time and O(nt N2) memory for the dense matrices, which is fine for a few thousand genes but not for much larger networks. Ranks use competition ranking for ties (1, 2, 2, 4).

    1.6 Baselines

    Betweenness (NetworkX, normalised), out-degree, PageRank (α = 0.85), driver personalised PageRank (restart only at the driver; the only baseline besides NetPert that sees the driver), and random scores. None of the baselines use the response genes.

    1.7 Simulated benchmark design

    ElementSetting
    Networks300 nodes; Barabási–Albert (m = 2) by default, plus Erdős–Rényi (mean degree 6), Watts–Strogatz (k = 4, p = 0.1) and 4-block stochastic block model; connected graphs only; each undirected edge becomes two directed edges
    DriverRandom choice among the 15 highest-degree nodes
    Responses20 nodes at shortest-path distance 3 or 4 from the driver (distance ≥ 2 if too few exist); 3–40 in Fig. 9
    Ground truthInterior nodes on any shortest path from driver to a response, excluding the responses
    EvaluationDriver and responses removed from scoring; AUROC (scikit-learn) and precision@20; mean ± 1.96 SD/√n over seeds (40 networks, or 20 in Figs. 8–9)
    Edge removal / addition5–50% of edges removed uniformly, or the same number of random non-edges added; 25 repeats on one network; Spearman ρ over all scored nodes and top-20 overlap with the unperturbed ranking
    RewiringDegree-preserving double edge swaps, 0.05–1.6 swaps per edge; 12 repeats
    Relaxation sweepr = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.99 (nt fixed at 16)

    1.8 Known weaknesses of this design

    Ground truth is defined by shortest paths, which is closer to what diffusion measures than to biology, and it favours methods that see the driver and responses. Simulated edges are symmetric, so regulatory directionality is untested. The robustness experiments use one base network, and seeds are fixed for reproducibility but results will shift with other seeds. Interval estimates are descriptive, with no multiple-testing correction. This page covers only the algorithmic core of NetPert, not the paper's data pipeline: network construction from IID and TRRUST, species mapping through MGI and UniProt, and drug-target scoring against the Drug Repurposing Hub. NetworkX 3.6.1 was used.

    2. Implementation check

    I wrote a vectorised version (one tensor contraction instead of triple loops) and a literal port of the repository's weight loop. On a 40-node test network their weights agree to a maximum absolute difference of 5.6e-17 (floating-point precision).

    2.1 Cross-check against the official code

    I then imported the official bin/netpert.py and called its own functions (getLaplacian, getTimeStep, getGlist, getWeights) on simulated networks, comparing the weights with my vectorised version. This covered 45 networks of 80 genes: undirected scale-free, directed scale-free and Erdős–Rényi graphs, each at three settings (r = 0.5 with 16 steps, r = 0.25 with 8, r = 0.9 with 32), 5 networks per cell, with 6 responses each.

    3. Benchmark against centrality baselines

    Over 40 random Barabási–Albert networks (300 nodes, 20 responses at distance 3–4 from the driver), the ground truth is the set of nodes lying on a shortest path from driver to a response. Values are mean ± 95% CI.

    MethodAUROCPrecision@20
    NetPert0.979 ± 0.0040.976 ± 0.016
    Betweenness0.823 ± 0.0120.675 ± 0.034
    Out-degree0.792 ± 0.0130.676 ± 0.036
    PageRank0.778 ± 0.0150.669 ± 0.034
    Random0.520 ± 0.0130.194 ± 0.024

    Caveat: NetPert is given the driver and responses, whereas the centrality baselines are network-wide and ignore them, so this comparison favours NetPert by construction. It shows that using the perturbation context helps, not that NetPert beats a driver-aware path-based method. A path-based ground truth also resembles what diffusion measures. It is also identical to the support of the paper's own driver-to-response betweenness comparator; section 20 uses an independent ground truth.

    4. Robustness to network errors

    Real interactomes are incomplete and noisy. On one 300-node network, I removed (or added at random) 5–50% of edges, 25 repeats per level, and compared rankings to the unperturbed ones.

    With 20% of edges removed, NetPert's mean Spearman ρ is 0.77 (betweenness 0.77); at 50% it is 0.47 (betweenness 0.57). Under random edge addition at 20%, they are 0.90 and 0.86. Rankings are therefore stable under mild noise and decay steadily, not abruptly, as the network degrades. NetPert is not clearly more robust than betweenness.

    5. Ranking structure and sensitivity to r

    The ranking is almost insensitive to r across 0.1–0.99, so the choice of relaxation fraction is not a major source of uncertainty.

    6. Extended visuals

    7. Further analyses

    These checks use only simulated networks, so they test the method's behaviour, not its biology. They include a driver-aware baseline (personalised PageRank from the driver), which addresses the unfairness noted in section 3.

    Takeaway. NetPert's advantage is real on these networks but depends on topology, and it is more sensitive than centrality baselines to rewired or missing edges. That matters for real interactomes, which are incomplete, so the Twist1 results should be judged with a driver-aware baseline and a stability check.

    8. Numerical verification and convergence

    Conservation identity. I checked the identity from section 1.4 numerically: summing Gbx(T−t) Gxa(t) over all genes x reproduces Gba(T) at all 17 time points, with a largest relative deviation of 3.4e−15. This confirms that the weights partition the driver-to-response influence.

    Quadrature convergence. Weights computed with nt = 2 to 64 time steps were compared with a 128-step reference.

    11. Robustness to realistic data problems

    This partly addresses the missing-directionality caveat, but the directions here are random, not biological. Real regulatory directions are correlated with gene function, so the real-data result may differ.

    Drag the slider (or press play) to watch activity spread from the driver through a 120-node network. Switch on the size option to see how the NetPert weights relate to where activity flows.

    In the animation the large black dot is the driver, blue diamonds are response genes, and other genes turn orange as activity reaches them. It shows the driver's linear diffusion on a simulated network. Time is scaled by the driver's out-degree, and it runs until 95% of the driver's activity has left it.     16. Glossary and FAQ

    Driver
    The perturbed gene (for the Twist1 example, Twist1).
    Response genes
    Genes whose expression changes after the perturbation.
    Mediator
    An intermediate gene that carries influence from the driver to the responses.
    Green's function
    The matrix exp(−tL) that gives each gene's activity at time t after a unit perturbation elsewhere.
    AUROC
    The probability that a random true mediator is ranked above a random non-mediator (0.5 = chance).
    Spearman ρ
    Rank correlation between two gene rankings.

    Why not just use betweenness? Betweenness ignores which genes were perturbed and which responded. NetPert uses both, which is why it wins on most of these tests, but a driver-aware baseline (driver PPR) closes part of the gap and wins on modular networks.

    Are these results biological? No. They show how the algorithm behaves on simulated networks with a known answer.

    Can I trust the top ranks? Only moderately: after removing 20% of edges about half of the top 15 genes stay in the top 20 (Fig. 11).

    17. Reproducibility and references

    Everything on this page comes from Python scripts using NumPy, SciPy (expm, romb), NetworkX 3.6.1, scikit-learn and Matplotlib, with fixed random seeds (network seeds 0–39, noted per experiment in section 1.7). The page does not offer downloads, so ask me for the scripts if you want to rerun them.

    • NetPert paper, PLOS Computational Biology (2024).
    • Official code repository, which is the reference for the weight calculation (bin/netpert.py).

    20. Independent ground truth and the paper's own comparators

    20.1 Why the earlier ground truth was too easy

    The benchmarks in sections 3–11 define mediators as genes on a shortest path from the driver to a response. The paper's own betweenness comparator (betweenness_centrality_subset with the driver as source and the responses as targets) is non-zero for exactly those genes, so it reaches AUROC 1.000 against that truth (last column below). Methods that look at paths are favoured, and my earlier "global" betweenness baseline was not the paper's comparator at all.

    20.2 Cascade-knockout ground truth

    The new truth does not use shortest paths or diffusion. Each directed edge is independently live with probability p = 0.5 (an independent cascade), and I sample 300 live-edge graphs per network. In each, a gene is critical for a response if it lies on every live path from the driver to that response (a dominator in the live graph). A gene's knockout effect is the expected number of the 20 responses that are lost when it is removed. Positives are genes with effect of at least 0.1 responses (on average 36 of 300 genes in the scale-free networks). I scored 40 scale-free networks, and 20 each of the other types.

    20.3 Comparators

    NetPert is my vectorised version (validated against the official code in section 2.1). BC (subset, paper) and TieDIE (paper) are computed by calling the official functions in bin/netpert.py the same way its all-methods routine does. I also kept global betweenness, out-degree and driver personalised PageRank.

    20.5 What this changes

    NetPert's advantage is real but modest once the ground truth is independent: it is a good all-round ranker by AUROC, not a dominant one, and a driver-and-response-aware betweenness is better at picking the very top genes. The large margins reported earlier mostly reflect a ground truth built from shortest paths.

    Caveats. The cascade model is itself a model, with one edge probability and independent edges. The 0.1 threshold and 300 samples are my choices, and results move with p (Fig. 21). Small-world networks have about 111 positives on average, against 10–36 elsewhere, so their AUROCs are not comparable across rows. None of this is real biology; it is still simulated.

    21. Accuracy on corrupted networks

    Real interactomes are incomplete, so the realistic test is how well each method recovers the true mediators when it only sees a degraded network. For 10 scale-free networks I computed the knockout truth (section 20) on the full network, then removed 10%, 20% or 40% of edges at random (5 repeats each) and scored every gene using the degraded network only. The comparators are run through the official code as in section 20.

    NetPert's AUROC falls from 0.905 on the full network to 0.880, 0.850 and 0.774 at 10%, 20% and 40% of edges removed. Out-degree falls more slowly (0.884, 0.873, 0.851, 0.818) and global betweenness too (0.869, 0.857, 0.838, 0.803). NetPert's lead is therefore gone by 20% removal and reversed at 40%. The paper's driver-and-response betweenness has the best precision@20 throughout (0.82 down to 0.67, against NetPert's 0.70 down to 0.60). TieDIE degrades fastest on precision@20 (0.73 to 0.46).

    Caveats. Only 10 networks and 5 repeats per level, so the intervals are wide and the 10–20% differences between NetPert and out-degree should not be over-read. Random edge removal is a mild model of missing interactions, since real missingness is biased towards poorly studied genes. This is still simulated data.

    22. Main experiments repeated with the independent truth

    Sections 7 and 11 used the shortest-path truth. Here I repeat them against the cascade-knockout truth (section 20), with the paper's comparators run through the official code. Each point uses 12 scale-free networks (20 for the directed test) with 300 genes, 20 responses unless stated, and a high-degree driver unless stated.

    22.4 Summary of the revised picture

    Against an independent truth, NetPert is most useful when the response list is short and clean, the driver is not a hub, and the network is directed. It loses its lead when the response list is long or contaminated with false positives (25% is enough), and when many edges are missing (section 21). Real response lists from expression data usually contain false positives, so the real-data run should include a noise sensitivity check.

    12 networks per point means wide intervals, so the smaller differences here are suggestive, not established. All results are simulated.

    23. Limitations and next steps

    Status: real-data run complete. The IID, TRRUST, MGI homology and Drug Repurposing Hub files were downloaded and the real Twist1 run is reported in section 0 above (full outputs: geneRankings_real.tsv, summary_real.json, 112-figure gallery). The simulation sections of this page remain behaviour tests with shortest-path ground truth, not evidence about drug targets.

    Follow-ups done since: the real Twist1 ranking, drug-target mapping, stability (edge-removal) and baseline analyses were all run on the real network (see section 0 and the 112-figure gallery).
